blocks.text: Quantization reduces the numeric precision used to store a model weights, representing each number with fewer bits, which shrinks memory usage substantially at the cost of some numeric accuracy, a tradeoff that underlies the QLoRA technique covered in the next several topics of this module.
This topic covers quantization as a general idea before the following topics dive into the specific 4-bit and NF4 techniques that make QLoRA practical.

Every number stored in a model, its weights, is represented using some fixed number of bits, and quantization converts those numbers from a higher precision representation, using more bits, to a lower precision one, using fewer bits, trading some numeric accuracy for a smaller memory footprint.

A weight stored as a 32-bit floating point number can represent an enormous range of values with fine granularity, while the same weight stored as an 8-bit integer can only represent 256 distinct values total, a dramatic reduction in precision in exchange for using one quarter the memory.

Since a model can contain billions of individual weights, even a small per weight memory reduction multiplies into an enormous total savings, a model stored in 4-bit precision uses roughly one eighth the memory of the same model stored in 32-bit precision.

code.content:
# A rough memory comparison, conceptually
def model_memory_gb(param_count, bits_per_param):
    return (param_count * bits_per_param) / 8 / 1e9

print(model_memory_gb(7e9, 32))  # full precision, larger
print(model_memory_gb(7e9, 4))   # 4-bit quantized, much smaller

blocks.text: Reducing precision inevitably introduces some rounding error, each weight gets approximated to the nearest representable value at the lower precision, and while modern quantization techniques minimize this error carefully, it can never be reduced to exactly zero, making this a genuine tradeoff rather than a free improvement.

Models commonly move through a range of precision levels, 32-bit floating point as the original full precision, 16-bit floating point as a common middle ground, 8-bit integers for more aggressive compression, and 4-bit representations, covered in depth in the next topic, for the most extreme memory savings.

blocks.text: Quantization was originally used mainly to shrink a fully trained model for cheaper, faster inference, but the technique underlying QLoRA extends it further, quantizing the frozen base model even during the fine-tuning process itself, not just afterward at deployment time.

QLoRA, the technique this module builds toward across its remaining topics, combines quantization of the frozen base model with LoRA low rank training on top, the base model sits in memory at a much lower precision than usual while the small trainable LoRA matrices, covered earlier in this module, still train normally, dramatically reducing the total memory needed for the entire fine-tuning process.

blocks.title: This is why QLoRA can fine-tune models that would not otherwise fit
blocks.content: A model that would not fit in available GPU memory at full precision can often fit comfortably once quantized, making QLoRA specifically valuable for fine-tuning large models on limited hardware, covered directly in a later topic of this module.

blocks.text: 8. Quantization Error and How It Accumulates

Every individual weight quantized introduces a small rounding error, and across an entire model, these small errors can compound, potentially degrading output quality if the quantization approach is naive, which is exactly why more careful quantization schemes, covered in the NF4 topic later in this module, were specifically developed to minimize this accumulated error.

Consider a weight with the value 0.7364. Quantized to a coarser representation that can only express increments of 0.1, it would be rounded to the nearest representable value, 0.7, a small individual error that, multiplied across millions or billions of weights, is the real cost quantization techniques work carefully to minimize.

A team wants to fine-tune a large model that does not fit in their available GPU memory at full 32-bit precision. By quantizing the frozen base model down to a much lower precision before training, they free up enough memory to fit both the quantized base model and the small trainable LoRA matrices, making the fine-tuning run possible on hardware that could never have handled it otherwise.

items: Assuming quantization is entirely free, without any tradeoff in numeric accuracy
Confusing quantization applied only at inference time with the training time quantization used in QLoRA
Not considering how quantization error can accumulate across billions of weights in a large model
Choosing an overly aggressive precision reduction without checking the resulting quality impact

blocks.text: For a model size of your choosing, calculate its approximate memory footprint at 32-bit, 16-bit, 8-bit, and 4-bit precision, confirming for yourself how dramatically the memory requirement shrinks at each step down.

Quantization reduces the number of bits used to store a model weights, trading some numeric accuracy for substantial memory savings, and combining a quantized frozen base model with LoRA training on top is exactly the idea behind QLoRA, making it possible to fine-tune models on hardware that could never accommodate them at full precision.
